Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

At a closing: Where a federally regulated lender must require it, the legal minimum is the loan balance or the NFIP's limit for the property, whichever is less (42 U.S.C. §4012a(b)). If such a lender notifies you that coverage is needed and you do not buy it within 45 days, the lender must buy it for you and can charge you for it (42 U.S.C. §4012a(e)). If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17). Buying a finished home with an NFIP building policy: the seller can assign the policy to you in writing when title transfers.

59.2% of North Carolina's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 59.2% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 18.7% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood insurance cost in North Carolina

In North Carolina, typically about $925 a year ($77 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $661 and $1,237. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $661 · Typical $925 · A quarter pay over $1,237 · A tenth pay $1,679 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 64,686 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $29.5 billion of building and $7.4 billion of contents coverage across all North Carolina policies.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Property that is not your primary residence, such as a second home, a rental you own or a non-residential building, pays a higher federal surcharge: $250 a year, against $25 for a primary home.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 3, 2026.

Source: floodsmart.gov, law.cornell.edu (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Exceptions in FEMA's flood insurance manual: with a loan secured by the insured property (making, increasing, extending or renewing it), coverage you apply for on or before closing can start at the time of the loan closing if the insurer gets the form and full amount due in time; the wait is one day when a FEMA map revision newly shows the building in a high-risk zone and the insurer gets them within 13 months of the revision's effective date. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Congress has to keep renewing the NFIP's authority. During a lapse, NFIP policies cannot be bought, renewed or increased until the authority returns. Policies already in force run to their expiration date and claims on them are still handled, though FEMA says the money to pay claims may be limited.

What it won't pay: The policy generally counts a flood only when water covers two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties, one of them yours. A standard NFIP home policy does not pay for a hotel or other living costs while you are out of the home, or for belongings outside the building, and it limits what it pays for in a basement. Belongings are paid at actual cash value (their used value), not the cost of new ones. Hurricanes can cause both wind and flood damage. A standard NFIP policy does not pay for wind damage, including rain blown in by wind or water coming through a roof the wind damaged; it does pay for water entering from the ground up, such as storm surge. Other policies, such as homeowners policies, may cover wind-driven rain, so you will likely file claims with both.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid after a flood goes to buy or build a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it for at least the amount of the aid, or you cannot get federal aid for later flood damage to it (44 CFR §206.110).

NFIP claim denied? You can appeal to FEMA within 60 days of the date on the denial letter, and you can sue within one year of the denial. An appeal does not extend that year. If repairs would cost 50 percent or more of the building's market value before the flood, it counts as substantially damaged under federal rules, and local floodplain rules can require elevating or other work. On an NFIP policy with building coverage, Increased Cost of Compliance pays up to $30,000 toward that; the local official's letter has to come before the work starts.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, ecfr.gov, law.cornell.edu, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in North Carolina: what floods pay out

Floods in North Carolina have led to 109,593 NFIP flood claims and $2.3 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2018, 2024 and 1999.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2018 ($644,871,042), 2024 ($260,302,214), 1999 ($230,319,296). Total paid $2,268,150,733. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 109,593 claims since 1978 against 130,556 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 39.7% of the 41,645 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 41,645 policies reporting one)39.7%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)77.9%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 80,441 claims paid with a damage figure)4.3%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 3, 2026.

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Why can a high-risk zone cost less than Zone X here? The premium is based on the flood risk of the building. The reason for any one zone is not in this data.

Why do sites quote different prices for North Carolina?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $925 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $832; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

36.0% of policies in North Carolina pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $723, full-risk $795 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$723
  • Median full-risk premium$795
  • Pay below full-risk36.0% of 64,686

Yearly cap: Except for the Emergency Program discount, statutory discounts gradually phase out through an annual increase cap discount at each renewal date until the policy reaches its full-risk premium. By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year; the rate for some property, including homes that are not a primary residence and business property, rises 25% a year until that group's average rate reaches the level the law sets (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)). FloodSmart puts the limit at 18 to 25% a year for most policyholders. It usually does not apply to new policies, raising your coverage or lowering your deductible can go past it, and fees and surcharges are added on top.

Paying a renewal 30 days or more after the policy expires causes a lapse in coverage. You then need a new application, and the lapse may cost you statutory discounts (what keeps a bill below full risk), including the yearly cap.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 3, 2026.

How often is North Carolina a flood disaster?

43 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Tropical Depression Chantal (2025).

  • September 2025 — Tropical Depression Chantal
  • October 2024 — Potential Tropical Cyclone Eight
  • September 2024 — Tropical Storm Helene
  • August 2024 — Tropical Storm Debby (emergency declaration)
  • October 2022 — Hurricane Ian (emergency declaration)
  • September 2021 — Remnants of Tropical Storm Fred

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $739.7 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,893 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 3, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.

In-force count: 130,556 policy units (from 115,066 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 115,066 of 115,066 fetched; claims: 109,593 of 109,593 fetched.
